title.text: Binondo Church (Minor Basilica of San Lorenzo Ruiz)

title_en.text: Binondo Church (Minor Basilica of San Lorenzo Ruiz)

tagline.text: A Chinatown minor basilica founded in 1596 for Chinese converts

location.label: Location
location.text: Plaza San Lorenzo Ruiz, Binondo, Manila

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0~300 (free entry; transport and snacks included, per person)

children.text: Binondo Church is the central church of Manila's Chinatown, founded by the Dominicans in 1596 for Chinese converts, and a minor basilica honoring Lorenzo Ruiz, the first Filipino saint. Its octagonal tower, the postwar-rebuilt nave and the plaza in front fit neatly into a one-hour visit.

The official name of Binondo Church is the Minor Basilica of San Lorenzo Ruiz, and parishioners also know it as the Parish of Our Lady of the Most Holy Rosary. It stands in the heart of Manila's Chinatown, Binondo, facing Plaza San Lorenzo Ruiz. According to Wikipedia, the Dominican Order founded the church here in 1596 to serve Chinese converts who had come from China as well as local Filipinos. The historical marker installed by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) in 1972 says Dominican priests built a mission for the Chinese in 1587 and that it became a parish in 1596, so some accounts date the beginnings to 1587.

There are two reasons the church is special. The first is its link to Lorenzo Ruiz, the first Filipino saint. Born in Manila, he was persecuted in Japan and was martyred without renouncing his faith. According to iDiscover Asia, he served as an altar boy at this church. The second is the architecture. The octagonal bell tower beside the church looks like a Chinese pagoda and carries the history of the neighborhood where Chinese Catholics settled. Wikipedia describes the tower as the only surviving part of the original 16th-century building.

The church has fallen and been rebuilt several times. The British invasion of 1762 destroyed the first building, the 1863 earthquake brought down the tower's top lookout (the mirador), and American bombing on September 22, 1944, near the end of World War II, destroyed most of it, leaving only the stone walls and the octagonal tower. For some years Mass was held in a roofless church before it was rebuilt in the 1950s, and the church and convent were renovated between 1946 and 1971. In 1992 Pope John Paul II approved its elevation to a minor basilica, and Cardinal Jaime Sin formally declared it on October 25 of that year. According to Wikipedia, the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines also raised it to a National Shrine on September 22, 2024.

Binondo Church does not demand much of your time as a traveler. After about an hour with the plaza, the nave, the tower and the side street, you are already at the food lane of Ongpin Street, so it works well as the starting point or a rest stop on a Binondo Chinatown walk. For photos, we recommend capturing the octagonal tower and the facade together from across the plaza. Remember that this is a working parish with daily Mass before it is a sightseeing spot, so moving quietly while you look around is basic courtesy.

The symbol of the church is its pagoda-like octagonal bell tower. Wikipedia says it is the only part that survived from the original 16th-century building and that its shape reflects the culture of the Chinese parishioners. The plaza is the best place to look up at it and take photos.

This church honors Lorenzo Ruiz, the first Filipino saint. iDiscover Asia says he was an altar boy here and that he never renounced his faith despite persecution in Japan. Knowing the story behind the church's name makes a visit far more meaningful.

This is the small plaza in front of the church. According to iDiscover Asia, it features a statue of Don Roman Ongpin, a Chinese businessman who helped the 1896 uprising against Spain. It is also the spot where you can see the facade and tower in a single view.

iDiscover Asia says the church floor is made of tombstone fragments engraved with Chinese and Latin text. It is a trace of Binondo's long history as a home to Chinese Catholics, so take a moment to look down as you walk.

blocks.title: Our Lady of the Rosary painting

children.text: According to the same guide, a side chapel holds a painting of Our Lady of the Most Holy Rosary, described as the oldest colonial painting in the country. Look around quietly, without disturbing worshippers at prayer.
According to Wikipedia, Masses here are held in Tagalog, Mandarin, Hokkien and English. The continuing faith life of Chinese Filipinos is very much part of Binondo's character.

Wikipedia says that Andrés Bonifacio, a leader of the Philippine revolution, and Gregoria de Jesús were married here in Catholic rites in the early 1890s (some say March 1893, others 1894). It shows that the church is tied to a scene from the city's history.

blocks.title: Traces of the 1944 bombing and rebuilding

children.text: The present nave was rebuilt after the 1944 bombing. Once you know it rose again from ruins where only the stone walls and the octagonal tower remained, the tidy facade looks different.
Arrive at Plaza San Lorenzo Ruiz and photograph the facade and the octagonal tower from across the plaza. Check out the statue of Don Roman Ongpin in the plaza as well.
Step inside and look around the nave quietly. If Mass is under way, watch from the back or shift your time a little. Take in the floor and the painting in the side chapel.
Leave the church and walk toward Ongpin Street. Grab a snack along the lane of Chinese restaurants, bakeries and herbal shops.
Continue to other sights in Binondo Chinatown (toward the Friendship Arch and Escolta), or have lunch.
Depending on Mass times, access inside the church may be limited, so check the parish Facebook page (@binondochurch1596) before you visit.

items.title: Half-day Binondo combination
items.subtitle: From the church to Chinatown and Intramuros

children.text: Look around Binondo Church first.
Walk the food lane along Ongpin Street.
Have lunch at an old Chinese restaurant or a local bakery.
Walk toward the Binondo–Intramuros Bridge and Jones Bridge and cross the Pasig River to Intramuros.
In the heat of midday, it helps to rest in the shade as you move.
If you start from central Metro Manila, LRT-1 Carriedo station and LRT-2 Recto station are nearby stations listed by Wikipedia. From the station, walk or ride a jeepney or tricycle to the church.
From the airport (MNL), a taxi or Grab to Binondo is the easiest way, but traffic can be heavy depending on the time of day, so leave with time to spare.
Stations and lines may change with construction or reorganization, so check the latest announcements.
The Binondo–Intramuros Bridge links Intramuros across the Pasig River to Binondo, and Wikipedia lists it among the sights around the church. Once across the bridge, it is a walk to the church plaza.
Grab or a taxi is the easiest way. Enter "Binondo Church" or "Plaza San Lorenzo Ruiz" in Google Maps to confirm the location.
Binondo has many narrow streets and traffic often backs up, so it is easier to get off near the church and walk.

The church is open year-round, but the dry season (December–May) has little rain and is good for walking the plaza and nearby lanes. In the rainy season, sudden showers fall some days, so bring an umbrella.
Weekends can draw crowds of worshippers and tourists, so choose a weekday if you want a quieter feel. Big events change the atmosphere, so check the parish's announcements before you visit.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Visit in the morning or at sunset to avoid the midday heat.
Bring an umbrella and allow extra time.

Binondo is the richest food neighborhood in Manila. A short walk from the church toward Ongpin Street brings you to shops selling dumplings, noodles, and Chinese-style bread and sweets. Many shops take cash, so it helps to carry small bills.

You can stay in a small hotel within Binondo, but if you only want to see the church, you can visit as a day trip from any hotel in central Manila. We recommend combining Intramuros, Escolta and Binondo in one day.
This is still a working parish with daily Mass. During Mass, enter quietly, watch from the back and refrain from taking photos.
Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is best. Avoid sleeveless tops and shorts.

Opening hours differ from site to site (for example, Mon–Sat 08:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:30, Sun 08:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 are one listing), so it is safest to confirm on the parish Facebook page (@binondochurch1596) or by phone (+63 2 8242 4850) before you go.
Sunday Mass is listed at about 08:30, 10:00, 12:15 and 17:00, but weekday and confession times vary by source. Check on site.
The tower and facade make a good composition when shot together from across the plaza.
Binondo is a walking neighborhood. Wear comfortable shoes and bring a hat and water by day.
There is a lot to see nearby, so plan about 1 hour for the church, 2 hours for the food lane and a half day for Intramuros or Escolta.
This is a crowded market district where pickpockets may operate, so keep your phone and wallet in front of your body.
Access inside the church may be limited during Mass and events.
The plaza and surrounding roads are busy, so watch for vehicles when you cross.
Parts of the interior may close for construction or events. Check the latest announcements.
Indiscriminate photography and flash can be disrespectful to worshippers.
Eat street food at your own careful discretion.
This is the whole Chinatown district where the church stands. From the church you can walk to the Ongpin Street food lane.
An old Manila commercial street reachable on foot from the church, listed by Wikipedia among the nearby sights.
The Spanish-era walled city reached by crossing the Binondo–Intramuros Bridge.
A large market district close to the church, listed by Wikipedia among the nearby sights.
